title: 'Meissner and Pacinian Corpuscles: Flutter and Vibration'

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: A flattened, Schwann-cell-like cell wrapped around a sensory terminal inside a corpuscle is a {{c1::lamellar cell}}.
cards.back: It is a non-neuronal partner of the sensory ending.
cards.quote: A lamellar cell is a flattened, Schwann-cell-like cell wrapped around the nerve terminal inside a corpuscle.

cards.front: An afferent whose firing dies away during a held press is {{c1::rapidly adapting}}.
cards.back: A release burst is common but is not required by the definition.
cards.quote: Rapidly adapting means that the firing dies away while a press is held.
cards.section: The typical response: a burst at each end

cards.front: Which rapidly adapting afferent classes do Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles carry, respectively?
cards.back: Meissner: RA I, detecting skin movement and low-frequency vibration. Pacinian: RA II, responding to higher-frequency vibration.
cards.quote: Meissner corpuscles carry the rapidly adapting type I (RA I) afferents, which detect movement across the skin and low-frequency vibration.
cards.section: The typical response: a burst at each end

cards.front: How did the human percepts and monkey afferent recordings in the flutter–hum study support a division of labour between Meissner and Pacinian afferents?
cards.back: Human flutter matched Meissner-type activity; hum matched Pacinian activity. The afferents were recorded in monkeys, so this was a comparison across preparations.
cards.why: The percept boundary describes a change in sensation, not a sharp receptor cut-off.
cards.quote: The comparison tied flutter to the rapidly adapting afferents now linked to Meissner corpuscles and the hum to Pacinian afferents.
cards.section: Flutter and hum

cards.front: Where did behavioural vibration sensitivity peak in the human index fingertip versus the mouse forepaw in the Prsa comparison?
cards.back: Near 240 Hz at the human index fingertip and near 1000 Hz in the mouse forepaw preparation.
cards.quote: behavioural vibration sensitivity peaked near 240 Hz at the human index fingertip and near 1000 Hz in their mouse forepaw preparation.
cards.section: Flutter and hum

cards.front: Two skin indentations have the same final size, but one builds over seconds and the other arrives in milliseconds. In the simple adaptation-filter model, which drives a rapidly adapting afferent more strongly, and why?
cards.back: The fast indentation drives it more strongly. Adaptation discounts slow change as the response dies away during the slowly building push.
cards.why: This comparison assumes the simple linear filter model; real firing also depends on amplitude, threshold and recovery.
cards.quote: a push that builds over seconds gives a smaller response than one that arrives in milliseconds.
cards.section: Flutter and hum

cards.front: A corpuscle has both capsule filtering and terminal adaptation. After capsule removal its spikes remain brief. Does that establish that the capsule had no role, and why?
cards.back: No. The remaining terminal adaptation can keep the output brief. The rule is that several stages can shorten a response, so a persistent transient does not isolate their individual contributions.
cards.quote: Because more than one place can make the response brief, removing one need not abolish it,
cards.section: Flutter and hum

cards.front: The established mammalian mechanically gated transducer in the sensory axon of Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles is {{c1::Piezo2}}.
cards.back: Force opens axonal channels to generate transduction current.
cards.quote: In mammals the established channel is Piezo2.
cards.section: Where force becomes current: Piezo2 in the axon

cards.front: How does force at a corpuscle become spikes in its sensory afferent?
cards.back: Force opens mechanically gated channels in the terminal. The resulting transduction current depolarizes the ending and drives action potentials.
cards.quote: Force opens mechanically gated channels in the afferent terminal, and the current that flows, the transduction current, is what drives spikes.
cards.section: Where force becomes current: Piezo2 in the axon

cards.front: In mouse Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles, axonal Piezo2 is needed for light-touch responses, but deleting Piezo2 from lamellar cells leaves those responses intact. Does this make lamellar cells dispensable?
cards.back: No. It identifies the required Piezo2 in the sensory axon. Preserved responses after lamellar-cell Piezo2 deletion do not exclude lamellar contributions through other mechanisms.
cards.quote: while deleting it from lamellar cells left those responses intact
cards.section: Where force becomes current: Piezo2 in the axon

cards.front: What distinguishes a corpuscle afferent’s generator potential from its impulses?
cards.back: The generator potential is graded depolarization at the ending. Impulses are all-or-none action potentials triggered further along the axon.
cards.quote: The generator potential is the graded depolarization of the nerve ending driven by the transduction current.
cards.section: Why the response is brief: capsule, terminal and spike

cards.front: What three stages can make a corpuscle afferent’s response to a held press brief?
cards.back: The capsule can reshape force, terminal channels can inactivate, and the spike generator can stop firing despite continued depolarization.
cards.quote: The spike generator. The membrane where impulses start could stop firing even while the ending stays depolarized.
cards.section: Why the response is brief: capsule, terminal and spike

cards.front: What did removing most capsule layers from isolated cat Pacinian corpuscles reveal about generator-potential adaptation versus impulse adaptation?
cards.back: Generator potentials decayed more slowly, mainly under intense compression, yet the ending typically fired only one spike. Mechanical filtering and impulse adaptation were separable.
cards.quote: The impulses did not persist: the ending typically still fired a single spike. So adaptation had two stages.
cards.section: The classical answer: the capsule

cards.front: During a held indentation, a sensory ending remains depolarized but its axon fires only once. Which adaptation stage is implicated, and why?
cards.back: The spike generator is implicated: firing stops despite a lasting generator potential. A brief spike train therefore does not establish that terminal depolarization was brief.
cards.quote: another lay in the terminal's spike-generating membrane, which stopped firing despite a lasting depolarization.
cards.section: The classical answer: the capsule

cards.front: How does the classical Pacinian capsule model turn a held press into brief onset and release signals?
cards.back: Force initially reaches the core; fluid flow and stretched layers then unload it during the hold. At release, elastic recoil jolts the core again.
cards.quote: During the hold the fluid flows and the stretched layers take up the load, so the core relaxes although the skin is still pressed.
cards.section: The classical answer: the capsule

cards.front: What did outer-core removal show in ex vivo Herbst corpuscles from late-stage duck embryos?
cards.back: Rapid terminal-current kinetics persisted, frequency tuning did not significantly change, and current amplitude increased. In this preparation, adaptation did not require the outer core.
cards.quote: Removing the outer core left the rapid kinetics of the mechanotransduction current intact and did not significantly change the afferent's frequency tuning.
cards.section: Testing the filter at the terminal itself

cards.front: After a corpuscle’s outer capsule is removed, terminal currents grow larger but decay just as rapidly. What role can still be assigned to the capsule, and why?
cards.back: It may damp stimulus strength even though rapid decay survives its removal. Current amplitude and adaptation kinetics describe different aspects of the response.
cards.quote: Decapsulation also increased the terminal's current amplitude, so the outer core may still damp the stimulus.
cards.section: Testing the filter at the terminal itself

cards.front: Why can a high-pass adaptation stage alone not explain a corpuscle afferent’s best vibration frequency?
cards.back: It suppresses slow inputs but has no peak. A best frequency also needs a limitation at high frequencies, such as mechanics, channel kinetics or spike timing.
cards.quote: A stage that discards slow change sets a graded low-frequency edge:
cards.section: Testing the filter at the terminal itself

cards.front: Cat decapsulation prolonged generator potentials, whereas healthy duck Herbst terminals retained fast currents after outer-core removal. Can the two results establish a universal capsule mechanism?
cards.back: No. They differ in species, preparation and recorded signal; deterioration can slow duck currents. The rule is to separate mechanics, terminal currents and spiking before assigning adaptation to one stage.
cards.quote: Slower inactivation appeared only as decapsulated terminals deteriorated, so a damaged, slowly dying terminal can look like a terminal that has lost its filter.
cards.section: Testing the filter at the terminal itself

cards.front: Why is the duck corpuscle described as bicellular rather than as an axon surrounded by passive padding?
cards.back: Both the afferent and lamellar cells can sense force, and lamellar-cell depolarization can influence afferent firing or mechanical threshold.
cards.quote: two kinds of cell, the afferent and the lamellar cells, each able to feel force and to influence the spike.
cards.section: What is left once the onion is gone: the lamellar cells

cards.front: In mice lacking the lamellar-cell membrane protein USH2A, Meissner RA I afferents lose much of their vibration sensitivity. What does this support?
cards.back: A lamellar-cell protein contributes to Meissner vibration sensitivity. The result does not identify the signal that couples the lamellar cell to the afferent.
cards.quote: without USH2A, a large membrane protein they carry, Meissner (RA I) afferents lose much of their vibration sensitivity
cards.section: What is left once the onion is gone: the lamellar cells

cards.front: Inhibiting mouse Pacinian lamellar Schwann cells raised awake mice’s vibration detection threshold about fivefold and reduced afferent responses. What does this establish about their normal coupling mechanism?
cards.back: They contribute to detection under the manipulation; it does not identify normal coupling. Artificial drive and expression in some other cell types limit the inference.
cards.quote: so the result shows that lamellar cells contribute to detection, not how they normally do it.
cards.section: What is left once the onion is gone: the lamellar cells

cards.front: A vibration is 200 Hz. How long is one cycle, and how many cycles fit into the shortest reported duck Grandry lamellar-cell-to-afferent delay of 20 ms?
cards.back: Period = 1/(200 Hz) = 0.005 s = 5 ms. Delay/period = 20 ms/5 ms = 4 cycles.
cards.why: A delay of four cycles does not by itself rule out cycle following: a constant delay can preserve timing.
cards.quote: A 200 Hz vibration repeats every 5 ms (1 ÷ 200 Hz = 0.005 s).
cards.section: What is left once the onion is gone: the lamellar cells

cards.front: Duck Grandry first-spike delays after lamellar-cell depolarization range from 20 ms to about 9 s. How would you test whether lamellar cells can relay individual vibration cycles?
cards.back: Apply repeated mechanical stimulation and measure timing in the same lamellar-cell–afferent pair. The rule is that cycle following requires cycle-to-cycle precision; first-spike latency under electrical drive does not measure that precision.
cards.quote: testing cycle following would need repeated mechanical stimulation and timing measured in the same cell–afferent pair.
cards.section: What is left once the onion is gone: the lamellar cells

cards.front: Which three molecular or signalling identities remain unresolved in the duck corpuscle account?
cards.back: The channel generating duck terminal currents, the lamellar-cell transducer, and the signal linking lamellar cell to terminal.
cards.quote: The channel behind the duck terminal currents, the lamellar-cell transducer and the signal from lamellar cell to terminal remain unidentified.
cards.section: What is left once the onion is gone: the lamellar cells

cards.front: Which two genetically distinct Aβ afferent populations usually share an adult mouse paw-pad Meissner corpuscle?
cards.back: A Ret-positive afferent and a TrkB-lineage afferent, intermingled among lamellar cells.
cards.quote: most corpuscles in adult mouse paw pads hold two genetically distinct Aβ afferents, intermingled among the lamellar cells.
cards.section: Two afferents in one Meissner corpuscle

cards.front: Why does a TrkB-lineage label in an adult mouse Meissner afferent not show that its terminal currently contains TrkB protein?
cards.back: The label records developmental expression. TrkB protein was undetectable in adult terminals, so lineage and current receptor expression are different claims.
cards.quote: TrkB protein was undetectable in adult terminals, so the TrkB label marks a developmental lineage, not a current receptor.
cards.section: Two afferents in one Meissner corpuscle

cards.front: A mouse paw-pad afferent keeps firing during maintained indentation and seldom fires at release. Does this response pattern rule out a Ret-positive Meissner identity, and why?
cards.back: No. Some Ret-positive units showed sustained firing and rarely responded at release. Calling both Meissner subtypes uniformly rapidly adapting overstates the mouse findings.
cards.quote: Ret-positive afferents were less sensitive and rarely fired at the release, and 4 of 10 recorded also fired during maintained indentation,
cards.section: Two afferents in one Meissner corpuscle

cards.front: Control mice detect a forepaw push at about 10 mN; developmental mutants lacking Meissner corpuscles detect it at about 20 mN. Calculate the threshold ratio and interpret detection capacity.
cards.back: Mutant/control = 20 mN/10 mN = 2.0. Threshold doubles, but remains measurable: normal sensitivity is impaired and other afferents can still support detection.
cards.quote: Adult control mice detected the push at a threshold of about 10 mN; mice lacking Meissner corpuscles, at about 20 mN
cards.section: Worked problem: a doubled threshold

cards.front: A sensory-neuron population is lost during development, yet adult animals still detect stronger touch. Would acute silencing of the population necessarily produce the same threshold shift, and why?
cards.back: No. Developmental loss can permit compensation or involve other afferents. The rule is that a developmental manipulation cannot determine the effect of acute silencing; either a larger or smaller shift remains possible.
cards.quote: other afferents may have compensated or contributed, and an acute silencing could give a larger or smaller effect.
cards.section: Worked problem: a doubled threshold

cards.front: How did vibration coding in mouse forelimb S1 differ from phase locking in the afferents supplying the signal?
cards.back: Afferents phase-locked to vibration; cortical neurons did not follow each cycle. Their firing rates encoded a feature combining frequency and amplitude.
cards.quote: The neurons did not fire in step with each cycle; their firing rates were tuned to a feature combining frequency and amplitude.
cards.section: Vibration in the brain and in the wild

cards.front: Near 440 Hz, vibration amplitude increases without a frequency change. How should perceived pitch shift in the mouse and human preparations, and why?
cards.back: Higher in mice and lower in humans. Amplitude pulls pitch toward best sensitivity: about 1000 Hz in mice and about 240 Hz in humans.
cards.quote: Near 440 Hz, below the mouse peak but above the human one, the two species therefore went opposite ways:
cards.section: Vibration in the brain and in the wild

cards.front: Awake, freely moving mouse Pacinian neurons respond to self-movement and external vibration. What does a response to substrate vibration generated 2.5 m away establish about distance sensitivity?
cards.back: The most sensitive neurons detected vibration at that distance on the tested surface. It was the furthest point tested, so it does not establish a detection limit.
cards.quote: the furthest point tested on that surface, not a known limit.
cards.section: Vibration in the brain and in the wild

cards.front: To isolate outer-core filtering from terminal mechanisms in a mouse Pacinian corpuscle, why compare currents and spikes before and after removal at matched terminal displacement?
cards.back: Matched terminal displacement controls the mechanical input; separate current and spike recordings locate downstream changes. The rule is that mechanics, transduction and impulse adaptation can each shorten the response.
cards.quote: so that any change in tuning can be assigned to mechanics or to the membrane.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: After dissection, sensory-terminal adaptation slows as leak current rises. What control would test whether capsule removal caused the slowing?
cards.back: Use sham-handled terminals kept for the same time and track leak in both groups. Slowing that follows deterioration would not isolate a capsule-filter effect.
cards.quote: If adaptation slows only as leak rises, deterioration, not loss of a filter, explains the change.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: The inner-core lamellar cells of a Pacinian corpuscle are {{c1::non-myelinating glia}}.
cards.back: The outer-core capsule layers are made by a different, non-glial cell type.
cards.quote: The outer-core layers of the Pacinian corpuscle are made by a different, non-glial cell type from the inner-core lamellar Schwann cells,
cards.section: Anatomy, terms and framing

cards.front: In an illustrative first-order high-pass model, corner frequency is 1/(2πτ). With τ = 9 ms, calculate the corner. Does its proximity to human flutter frequencies identify the human mechanism?
cards.back: τ = 0.009 s; corner = 1/(2π × 0.009 s) ≈ 17.7 Hz. No: this duck-derived illustrative model offers only a cross-species order-of-magnitude coincidence.
cards.quote: With τ = 9 ms, the onset inactivation time constant of the duck Grandry terminal current, the corner is 1/(2π × 0.009 s) ≈ 17.7 Hz.
cards.section: A simple filter model of adaptation

cards.front: How did Grandry lamellar cells and Herbst outer-core cells differ in excitability in ex vivo duck bill recordings?
cards.back: Grandry lamellar cells fired action potentials. Herbst outer-core cells were mechanosensitive but not excitable.
cards.quote: Herbst outer-core cells were mechanosensitive but not excitable.
cards.section: Duck bill recordings, step by step

cards.front: Mouse TrkB-lineage Meissner endings have more lamellar wrappings than Ret-positive endings. How could you test the proposal that wrapping changes threshold through mechanics rather than terminal kinetics?
cards.back: Compare terminal displacement and currents across the two types at matched displacement, alongside force thresholds. The rule is that wrapping may alter force delivery, whereas current kinetics describe terminal behaviour; wrapping–threshold correlation alone does not distinguish them.
cards.quote: the authors proposed that the extent of wrapping helps set an afferent's force threshold and kinetics.
cards.section: Meissner afferent labels, tallies and wrapping

cards.front: For the local mouse fit P = f × (A/Aref)^0.32 with Aref = 5.6 µm, what frequency at 11.2 µm matches 450 Hz at 5.6 µm? Assume the fit holds at double amplitude.
cards.back: Equal pitch gives f = 450 Hz/2^0.32 ≈ 360.5 Hz: a 19.9% decrease. The amplitude ratio is dimensionless. This extrapolates the local mouse fit; it is not a new measurement.
cards.quote: This is a prediction of a local mouse fit, assumed to hold at double amplitude; it is not a new measurement.
cards.section: Worked problem: the equal-pitch fit
